content: # Why has my car burnt through all the oil? A Vauxhall Corsa 1.2 from 2013 consuming an entire oil reservoir between two top-ups is a textbook example of catastrophic internal failure, specifically regarding the engine's sealing integrity. When you see white smoke pouring from the exhaust and lose power simultaneously, the diagnostic logic becomes clear: the combustion chamber is no longer isolated from the crankcase. In your specific scenario, where the AA identified oil burning after a recent top-up, and subsequent attempts to replace ignition coils and spark plugs failed to restore performance or stop the consumption, we can narrow down the root cause significantly. Ignition components manage the spark; they do not control fluid pressure or piston ring movement. If the car still has no power after replacing these parts, the mechanical failure lies deeper within the block itself. The most probable culprit is worn piston rings or a damaged cylinder wall. In a 2013 model with roughly 11 years of age, normal wear and tear can lead to ring end gaps widening or carbon buildup preventing the rings from sealing against the bore. When these seals fail, oil bypasses the rings and enters the combustion chamber. Once inside, this oil burns during the ignition cycle, creating white or bluish smoke and diluting the fuel mixture, which explains the sudden loss of power. Another possibility is a failed valve stem seal. These rubber O-rings sit atop the valves to prevent oil from dripping down into the cylinders when the engine is off or idling. If these seals degrade due to age or heat cycles, oil leaks past the guide and into the combustion chamber. While this often manifests as blue smoke on startup that clears after warming up, severe degradation can lead to constant burning. A third, less common but critical failure point is the turbocharger (if equipped) or the Positive Crankcase Ventilation (PCV) system. If your Corsa has a direct injection engine paired with a small turbo, the turbo shaft seals can wear out, allowing crankcase pressure to blow oil into the intake tract. Similarly, if the PCV valve is clogged or stuck closed, excessive pressure builds up in the crankcase and forces oil past the piston rings through the ring grooves. The garage's suggestion of a new engine implies they ruled out simple external leaks (like a cracked gasket) but found no other mechanical fault codes. Before committing to a full engine replacement, you must verify which sealing component has failed. A compression test and a leak-down test are essential here. These tests measure the ability of each cylinder to hold pressure. If compression is low across all cylinders, it points to ring failure or excessive bore wear. If one specific cylinder fails the test while others pass, it likely indicates a blown head gasket or a localized valve seal issue. If the diagnostics confirm internal wear, replacing the engine is indeed the only viable repair option for a 1.2-liter naturally aspirated unit from this era. The cost of machining a block to restore ring lands and honing cylinders often exceeds the value of the vehicle. However, if the head gasket is blown, a professional resurface job might be an alternative, though labor-intensive. Given the severity of the situation where oil was completely consumed, ignoring this will lead to total engine seizure as metal-on-metal contact destroys the crankshaft and bearings. The decision matrix here is simple: if the vehicle is under warranty or has a strong history, consider a replacement unit with a certified rebuild; otherwise, if the car is near its economic limit, a used engine swap might be the pragmatic choice, provided you source one from a reliable donor to avoid inheriting similar issues.
